stanzas: Lully, lulla, þᵂ littell tiné child,
O sisters too, how may we do
This pore yongling for whom we do singe
Herod, the king, in his raging,
His men of might in his owne sight
That wo is me, pore child, for thee,
For thi parting nether say nor singe,
orig.credit: Traditional; Robert Croo's text of 1534 in Thomas Sharp's transcription (1825), as quoted in Wikipedia's article

stanzas: Lully, lulla, you little tiny child,
O sisters two, what can we do
this poor little one for whom we sing
Herod the king, in his raging,
to his men of might, in his own sight,
So that I am full of woe, poor child, for you,
for your parting, neither speak nor sing

notes: Sharp's 'þᵂ' is 'thou', 'þⁱˢ' 'this'; 'lully, lulla, lullay' and 'by by' are lullaby sounds, kept.
2.1: 'too' is generally read as 'two' (the mothers of the pageant).
4.1: 'That wo is me' read as 'so that woe is me'.
4.3: the sense is uncertain: perhaps 'at your parting I can neither speak nor sing "bye bye, lully, lullay"'.
